items.answer: Pressing the handle opens a valve at the tank's bottom.
items.why: This valve controls the flow of water into the bowl.
items.scene: A metal gate swings open like a tiny door when you push the handle.

check.wrong: The handle directly pushes water into the bowl.
check.right: The handle opens a valve that lets water flow.

items.answer: Water pours from the tank into the bowl quickly.
items.why: Gravity pulls the water down, creating a strong flow.
items.scene: A waterfall of water cascades from the tank into a waiting bowl below.

check.wrong: Water trickles slowly into the bowl.
check.right: Gravity makes water rush quickly from tank to bowl.

items.answer: The water in the bowl drains away through a pipe.
items.why: The drain line pulls the waste and water out of the bowl.
items.scene: A hidden pipe under the bowl sucks everything away like a vacuum.

check.wrong: The water stays in the bowl after flushing.
check.right: The drain immediately pulls water and waste away.

items.answer: The draining water creates a suction that pulls waste away.
items.why: As water leaves, it lowers pressure, pulling everything with it.
items.scene: A tiny whirlpool forms in the bowl as waste disappears.

check.wrong: Water alone removes the waste without suction.
check.right: Draining water creates suction that pulls waste with it.

items.answer: Once empty, the tank begins refilling automatically.
items.why: The valve at the bottom closes, and the fill valve opens again.
items.scene: The tank's gate slams shut, and a faucet above starts dripping.

check.wrong: The tank never refills after one flush.
check.right: The tank automatically refills once the flush is complete.

results.topic: How noise-cancelling headphones work

deck.title: How noise-cancelling headphones work
deck.subtitle: 5 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Microphones capture surrounding sound waves as electrical signals.
items.why: Sound waves vibrate the microphone's diaphragm, creating measurable electrical changes.
items.scene: A tiny spider-web microphone nestles between your ear and the world.

check.wrong: Microphones just amplify the sound you hear.
check.right: Microphones convert sound vibrations into electrical signals for processing.

items.answer: The processor compares incoming sound to a quiet reference signal.
items.why: Finding the inverse of the noise allows it to be subtracted out.
items.scene: A tiny wizard in the headphone circuit scribbles anti-noise spells.

check.wrong: The processor simply turns down the volume of all sounds.
check.right: The processor calculates an exact inverse signal to cancel specific noise.

items.answer: The processor creates a sound wave that is the exact opposite of the noise.
items.why: When noise and its inverse meet, they cancel each other out.
items.scene: Two waves, one black and one white, collide and vanish.

check.wrong: Anti-noise is just silence played back to you.
check.right: Anti-noise is a precise sound wave that destructively interferes with noise.

items.answer: The headphone speaker plays the anti-noise directly into your ear.
items.why: The anti-noise meets the noise at your eardrum and cancels it.
items.scene: A tiny speaker whispers the exact opposite of every outside whisper.

check.wrong: The speaker only plays music, not the anti-noise.
check.right: The speaker continuously plays both music and precisely timed anti-noise.

items.answer: The noise and anti-noise waves cancel each other, leaving quiet.
items.why: Destructive interference removes unwanted sound pressure at your ear.
items.scene: A noisy street wave hits your ear and dissolves into calm.

check.wrong: Cancellation just makes all sound quieter for everyone nearby.
check.right: Cancellation only removes specific noise frequencies reaching your ear, not others'.

results.topic:
Water cycle notes (Year 9 geography)
- sun heats oceans/lakes -> evaporation, water vapour rises
- plants lose water from leaves = transpiration
- vapour cools higher up -> condenses on dust -> clouds
- droplets join, get heavy -> precipitation (rain, snow, hail)
- runoff over ground into rivers, some soaks in = infiltration -> groundwater
- rivers + groundwater flow back to sea, cycle repeats

deck.title: Water Cycle Journey
deck.subtitle: 6 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Sun heats water, turning it to vapor that rises.
items.why: Heat makes water molecules move faster and escape into air.
items.scene: A giant hairdryer blows on a swimming pool, making steam dance upward.

check.wrong: Only oceans evaporate, not lakes or rivers.
check.right: All surface water evaporates when the sun heats it.

items.answer: Plants push water vapor from leaves into the air.
items.why: This adds more water vapor to the air around us.
items.scene: A giant green monster wigs out, spraying mist from its hair.

check.wrong: Transpiration is just water dripping from leaves.
check.right: Transpiration releases vapor, not liquid, into the air.

items.answer: Cool air makes vapor condense into tiny droplets on dust.
items.why: Cool temperatures slow molecules, letting them stick together.
items.scene: Breath fogs a cold window, leaving tiny water droplets on glass.

check.wrong: Clouds form from water falling directly from the sky.
check.right: Clouds form when vapor condenses on particles in the air.

items.answer: Tiny droplets clump together to make visible clouds.
items.why: Clumping creates structures big enough to scatter light and appear.
items.scene: A snow globe shakes, and tiny snowflakes clump into fluffy clouds.

check.wrong: Clouds are made of ice only, not water droplets.
check.right: Clouds are mostly tiny water droplets, sometimes with ice.

items.answer: Heavy water droplets fall as rain, snow or hail.
items.why: Gravity pulls them down when they are too heavy to stay.
items.scene: A bucket overflows, dripping ice cubes, water drops and snow.

check.wrong: Rain falls only when it is hot outside.
check.right: Precipitation occurs in many temperatures, as rain, snow or hail.

items.answer: Runoff flows to rivers, infiltration soaks into groundwater, both reach oceans.
items.why: Gravity and soil absorption move water back to start the cycle.
items.scene: A garden hose splashes on dirt, feeding a stream and soaking roots.

check.wrong: Groundwater never reaches the ocean again.
check.right: Groundwater flows slowly back to oceans to restart the cycle.

results.topic: Why is the sky blue?

deck.title: Why the sky is blue
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Sunlight bounces off air molecules in many directions.
items.why: Air molecules scatter shorter blue light more than longer red light.
items.scene: Tiny invisible dancers scattering blue glitter from a flashlight beam.

check.wrong: The sky is blue because the sun is blue.
check.right: The sun is yellow; blue light scatters more in our atmosphere.

items.answer: Blue light spreads more than other colors when it hits air.
items.why: Shorter blue light waves bounce off molecules more easily than longer red waves.
items.scene: Blue ribbons fluttering wildly in a gentle breeze, red ribbons barely moving.

check.wrong: All colors spread the same in the air.
check.right: Blue light scatters more than red or yellow light.

items.answer: Our eyes are most sensitive to the scattered blue light.
items.why: Human eyes detect blue light strongly, making the sky appear blue.
items.scene: A baby looking up, seeing a bright blue balloon against white clouds.

check.wrong: We see the sky as blue because space is blue.
check.right: Space is black; we see blue because of scattered sunlight.

items.answer: At sunset, light travels farther, scattering blue away and leaving red.
items.why: Longer path through air removes more blue light, letting red reach us.
items.scene: A orange cat sleeping as the sun dips behind red cliffs.

check.wrong: Sunsets are red because the sun turns red.
check.right: Sunsets appear red due to longer light paths scattering blue light.
